courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Probes: kprobes, tracepoints, fentry, uprobes and profile
question: In a kretprobe on a function, you try to print arg0 to see which file descriptor was passed in. What goes wrong, and what fixes it?
options: Arguments are not available at return in a kretprobe; save them in a map keyed by tid at entry, or use fexit, which still has args
Nothing; arg0 is preserved for kretprobe
kretprobes cannot access any data at all; use printf instead
You must cast arg0 to a pointer first
explain: A kretprobe only has retval: argument registers may have been overwritten by the time the function returns. Save what you need at entry, keyed by tid, or use fexit, whose args remain available on return.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
question: A colleague's kprobe-based script worked last year but now fails to attach after a kernel upgrade. What is the most likely cause?
options: The verifier became stricter about printf
bpftrace no longer supports kprobes
Tracepoints replaced all kprobes
The probed kernel function was renamed, removed or changed, because kprobes target internal, unstable functions
explain: kprobes can attach to almost any kernel function, but those functions are not an API. Tracepoints, or fentry with BTF types, are more resilient. By default bpftrace exits with an error if any probe fails to attach, unless the missing_probes config is set to warn or ignore.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Per-channel scales, calibration, and quantization-aware training
question: Why do the gradients in QAT use the straight-through estimator instead of the true derivative of round()?
options: The true derivative is zero almost everywhere, so no gradient would reach the weights
round() is not implemented on GPUs
The estimator makes training faster but changes the final model format
It removes the need for calibration
explain: round() is a step function: its derivative is zero except at the jumps, where it is undefined. Treating the quantizer as identity inside the clipping range lets gradients flow so the float weights can move to positions that quantize well.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Length penalties inside RL: Kimi k1.5 and DAPO
question: In a GRPO group, all 8 sampled responses are correct but their lengths differ. With correctness reward only, what is the policy gradient signal from this group?
options: Zero: every reward is equal, so every advantage is 0, and length gets no push either way
Strongly favors the shortest response
Strongly favors the longest response
Negative for all responses, since the mean is subtracted
explain: Equal rewards give zero advantages, so the group teaches nothing. Kimi's length reward breaks the tie inside such groups, which is exactly where length can be cut without hurting accuracy.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Running edge detection and ON/OFF matching on the toy house
question: Which change to the toy pipeline would most directly avoid the minute-45 failure?
options: Raise the edge threshold from 30 W to 70 W
Use more clusters in k-means
Sample faster so the lamp-off and fridge-on events fall in different samples
Use the cluster median instead of the mean as each appliance's power
explain: The failure comes from two events sharing one sample. Faster sampling separates them into two clean edges (-60 then +120). A 70 W threshold would drop the +64 edge but also the lamp's real +51 ON edge, and the fridge would still have no ON edge at 45. More clusters or a median do not undo a merged edge.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Cleaning: Unicode, case, punctuation and legal suffixes
question: Which single step makes `Ｑｕａｎｔｉｘ` (full-width) equal to `Quantix`?
options: Case folding with casefold()
Unicode NFC normalization
Unicode NFKC normalization
Removing punctuation
explain: Full-width letters are compatibility characters. Only the K forms (NFKD, NFKC) apply compatibility mappings; NFC handles canonical equivalence only and leaves them unchanged. Case folding does not map full-width letters to ASCII.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Job titles: taxonomies, seniority and embeddings
question: Why store seniority in a separate field instead of making `Senior Software Engineer` its own taxonomy entry?
options: Taxonomies cannot store adjectives
So that an occupation filter matches every level, and level can be filtered independently, without multiplying entries per occupation
Because embeddings cannot encode seniority
explain: Combining occupation and level multiplies entries and splits recall: a filter for software developers would have to enumerate every level. Two fields keep both filters simple and avoid one taxonomy entry per occupation and level.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
question: A level-triggered server registers every connection with EPOLLIN | EPOLLOUT and leaves it that way. CPU sits at 100 percent even with no traffic. Why?
options: EPOLLOUT is invalid without EPOLLET
Idle sockets almost always have send-buffer space, so each one is reported writable on every epoll_wait and the loop never sleeps
epoll_wait ignores the timeout when EPOLLOUT is set
The kernel rescans the interest list on every call
explain: Level-triggered means "report while the condition holds". Writable is true for nearly every idle socket, so every wait returns immediately with work that is not real. Register EPOLLOUT only while you have unsent data (EPOLL_CTL_MOD), or use ET.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Split by query and keep a rotating sealed test set
question: Why does the MS MARCO document leaderboard score every submission on 45 extra queries that never appear on the public board?
options: To give the organizers a held-out check on whether public gains carry over to queries no one could tune on
To raise the total number of evaluation queries so the public score is more precise
Because TREC labels are too expensive to show publicly
To break ties on the public leaderboard
explain: A private set that no participant receives feedback on cannot be adaptively overfit. If teams were climbing the public board by tuning to its queries, their runs would gain publicly and slip on the private queries.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Non-executable memory: the NX bit, DEP and W^X
question: A program is built with NX but not with a stack canary. An overflow replaces the return address with the address of the overflowing buffer itself, which holds attacker bytes. What happens at ret?
options: The injected bytes run, because NX only protects the heap
The return address is restored by NX
ret jumps to the stack, the CPU refuses to execute from a non-executable page, and the process faults
The compiler refuses to compile the overflow
explain: NX does not prevent the hijack; it prevents the hijacked jump from running data. The process faults on the instruction fetch from the stack page. The return address was still corrupted, which is why attackers moved to reusing code that is already executable (next lesson).

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: RELRO, the GOT and FORTIFY_SOURCE
question: Which overflow can FORTIFY_SOURCE catch?
options: memcpy into a local `char buf[64]` with a length taken from the network that exceeds 64
A for loop that copies bytes one by one past the end of a local array
A use-after-free of a heap object
An overflow inside a function compiled at -O0
explain: FORTIFY rewrites calls to listed library functions when the destination size is known; memcpy into a fixed local array is the textbook case. It does nothing for hand-written loops, lifetime bugs like use-after-free, or code built without optimization.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Kernel mitigations: SMEP, SMAP, KASLR, KPTI and EternalBlue
question: According to Microsoft's analysis, which change made EternalBlue as leaked fail on the newest 64-bit Windows 10 even before patching?
options: The HAL region it relied on was no longer executable and its address was randomized
SMBv1 was removed from Windows 10
Windows 10 used stack canaries in the kernel
The NSA patched the exploit
explain: The exploit placed its payload in the HAL region at a known, executable address, which held on Windows 7. Windows 10 made that memory non-executable and the latest 64-bit builds randomized it. The SMBv1 bug itself remained until MS17-010 was applied.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
question: Two threads write different fields of one struct that fits in a single cache line. A colleague says this cannot be slow because nothing is shared. What is the best reply?
options: Right, the compiler places each field on its own line automatically
Right, only atomic variables can cause cache contention
Wrong, but only because the struct needs a mutex
Wrong, the fields share one cache line, so each write forces the line to move between cores
explain: Compilers pack fields together to save space; they do not spread them across lines. Any write needs the whole line, so the two cores fight over it. No mutex is needed for correctness here, because the fields are distinct; the problem is purely performance.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: How big is a line, how to find false sharing, who pads
question: Why might a library avoid the C++17 constant `hardware_destructive_interference_size` in a public header?
options: Its value can change with compiler tuning flags, so separately built code may disagree on struct layout
It is not defined in C++17
It is always 64, which is too small
It only works with std::atomic members
explain: GCC sets it from -mtune, and its documentation warns that all translation units relying on it must use the same tuning. In a public header that is an ABI hazard, so libraries often use a fixed constant such as 128 instead.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Non-IID data and client drift: fast convergence to the wrong answer
question: A colleague says FedAvg with E = 5 was fine on their IID benchmark, so the non-IID result must be a bug. What is the right response?
options: They are right: FedAvg is split-independent by construction
With IID clients every local optimum equals the global one, so there is nothing to drift toward; the skew is what creates the bias
The IID result must also be biased, just less visibly
Drift only appears when clients have different sample counts
explain: In our IID split every client has curvature 10/3 and local optimum 2.3, so the fixed point is 2.3 for any E and larger E is pure speedup. Unequal sample counts alone are harmless, since FedAvg already weights by n_k; what hurts is local objectives that disagree with the pooled one.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: Paying for density: M_beta compression and two-hop recovery
question: During compression, candidate d is pruned from v's list because it is in H. At search time, under a predicate where d passes but kept neighbor c (which links to d) fails, can the search still reach d from v?
options: No, because c fails the predicate and is skipped
Yes, if c sits beyond position M_beta, because the lookup expands c's list before filtering
Only if d is within the first M_beta entries
Only with ACORN-1
explain: The two-hop expansion reads c's neighbor list regardless of whether c passes; the predicate is applied to the expanded entries. By construction, any pruned node was in H only because some later kept neighbor links to it, and entries past M_beta are exactly the ones the lookup expands.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Aux-loss-free balancing: steer the router with a bias
question: A colleague's implementation computes `weights = gather(s + b, pick)` and multiplies expert outputs by those weights. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; using the biased score everywhere is the method
The top-K must be taken on s alone, and the bias added after
The bias should be multiplied, not added
The bias now changes each expert's contribution to the output, so a balancing knob leaks into the model's function; gates must use the raw scores s
explain: The paper and DeepSeek-V3 both state that the bias is only used for routing; the gate value comes from the original affinity. With the bug, an underloaded expert's output is inflated just because it was underloaded, which distorts the forward pass. (A multiplicative bias was tested and was slightly worse, but it too only affects selection.)

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-3: producer and consumer warps, then ping-pong
question: A teammate proposes giving the producer warpgroup as many registers as the consumers, "to be fair." What is the most likely effect?
options: Faster loads, because TMA needs registers for each byte copied
No effect, because register counts are fixed per kernel
Fewer registers for the consumers, forcing smaller tiles or spills in the math path
Better ping-pong, because both warpgroups can then do softmax
explain: TMA is issued by a single thread and copies data without staging it in registers. Registers given to the producer are taken from the consumers, which hold the accumulators; the paper deallocates producer registers and reallocates them to consumers for exactly this reason.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Why LLM serving needs its own attention engine
question: Which of these does FlashInfer treat as run-time input to its scheduler rather than as a compile-time kernel parameter?
options: The head dimension
Whether logits are soft-capped
The KV length of each request in this step
The data type of the KV cache
explain: Head dimension, the variant (such as soft-capping) and dtypes are fixed when the kernel is JIT compiled. Per-request lengths change every step, so they go to the plan function, which produces a fresh work assignment without recompiling.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants
question: You want attention with RoPE applied inside the kernel (instead of a separate RoPE pass that writes rotated Q and K to HBM). Which variant hooks do you implement?
options: LogitsMask
OutputTransform
QueryTransform and KeyTransform
ValueTransform only
explain: RoPE rotates query and key vectors before their dot product, which is exactly what the query and key transform functors are for. The paper uses them for fused RoPE in StreamingLLM. A mask or output hook acts too late, and values are not rotated.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Relation to diffusion, and rectified flow in Stable Diffusion 3
question: Why does SD3 sample training timesteps from a logit-normal instead of uniformly?
options: The velocity regression is easiest near t = 0 and t = 1, so spending more training samples on intermediate t gives a better model
Uniform sampling makes the ODE solver unstable at test time
Logit-normal sampling removes the need for classifier-free guidance
It makes the paths straight without reflow
explain: Esser et al. argue that near the ends the target is easy to predict (close to pure data or pure noise), and confirm experimentally that rf/lognorm(0.00, 1.00) beats uniform rectified flow. It reweights the loss over time; it does not change the paths or the sampler.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Model checking a consensus core: votes, quorums and restarts
question: Which configuration makes TLC report a OneValue violation even with AllowRestart = FALSE?
options: 3 acceptors, quorum size 2
5 acceptors, quorum size 3
5 acceptors, quorum size 4
4 acceptors, quorum size 2
explain: Two quorums can be disjoint when 2 x QSize <= number of acceptors. With 4 acceptors and size 2, {a1, a2} and {a3, a4} share no one, so each can choose a different value. TLC's trace is 4 votes long.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Fine-grained FP8 at scale: tiles, blocks and FP32 promotion
question: Why does DeepSeek-V3 scale activations per 1x128 tile instead of per tensor?
options: A single outlier would set the scale for the whole tensor and push ordinary values toward FP8's subnormal range; small tiles confine each outlier to its own 128 values
Tensor cores cannot read a per-tensor scale
Tiles let the model skip the Wgrad GEMM
Per-tile scales make the format exact, so no rounding happens
explain: Fine-grained scaling limits each outlier's damage to its own tile, so every other tile can use E4M3's full range. That is also what lets DeepSeek use E4M3 everywhere instead of E5M2 for gradients.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
question: A log appends a 200-byte record to the end of a file, then calls `fdatasync()`. Which change may still be left unflushed?
options: The file's new size, since size is metadata
The modification time (st_mtime)
The record bytes themselves
Nothing: fdatasync and fsync are identical on Linux
explain: fdatasync skips metadata that is not needed to read the data back. The new size is needed (otherwise a reader would not see the appended bytes), so it is flushed. The modification time is not needed, so it can stay dirty. That saving is the whole point of fdatasync.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: When fsync lies or fails: drive caches and fsyncgate
question: A server runs PostgreSQL with default settings on an SSD whose volatile write cache ignores flush commands. The power fails. What does WAL guarantee for transactions that were reported committed?
options: They survive, since fsync returned success for their commit records
They survive, because full_page_writes protects them
Nothing reliable: WAL relies on the flush being honest, so recently acknowledged commits, or even WAL before data ordering, can be lost
Only that they will be redone from the data files
explain: Every guarantee in this course rests on the device persisting data when it says it has. If the drive acknowledges a flush that only reached volatile cache, both durability and the write-ahead ordering can break. The fix is in hardware or configuration, not in the database.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: A real hunt with libFuzzer: harness, run log and the crash
question: Why does the harness allocate the struct with calloc inside LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput instead of using one global struct?
options: calloc is faster than a global
libFuzzer forbids global variables
Globals cannot be written by memcpy
A fresh object per run keeps runs independent and lets ASan put redzones around exactly 20 bytes
explain: State left over from a previous input makes results irreproducible, and a heap object gets ASan redzones right after its last byte. (A global would also get redzones, but leftover state between runs is the bigger problem.)

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Crash triage: deduplicate, minimise, root-cause, fix
question: Why does the fix return -1 for len > 16 instead of copying only the first 16 bytes?
options: Truncation is slower
memcpy cannot copy fewer bytes than requested
Returning -1 is required by ASan
Silently truncating hides malformed input from the caller and changes data without telling anyone; rejecting makes the error visible
explain: Both stop the overflow. Rejecting keeps the parser honest about invalid input. Truncation can be right for some formats, but it should be a deliberate decision, documented and tested.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Protocol and stateful fuzzing, and the Broadcom Wi-Fi case
question: A fuzzer for a Wi-Fi chip mutates single management frames from a fresh, unassociated state and finds nothing in a week. What is the most likely gap?
options: The firmware has no bugs
Wi-Fi cannot be fuzzed
The sanitizer is missing
The vulnerable handlers run only in later states (associated, TDLS set up), which single frames from the start state never reach
explain: As in the Broadcom research, the interesting parsers sit behind protocol state. Replay a valid setup sequence, then mutate the frames that arrive afterwards.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing the report and coordinating disclosure
question: Which item does NOT belong in a first private report of a memory-safety bug?
options: The minimised reproducer and sanitizer output
The affected versions and a root-cause sentence
A suggested fix or pointer to guidance
A demand for payment before you share details
explain: OWASP warns that demanding payment as a condition of reporting can be extortion. Rewards belong in an established bug bounty programme with published terms.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Jaro-Winkler, trigrams and token scorers on the same pairs
question: You match company names where one source often adds suffixes such as LLC or Inc and words are sometimes reordered. Which scorer handles both cases, and what must you watch for?
options: fuzz.ratio; it is the most precise
Jaro-Winkler; it rewards shared prefixes
partial_ratio; it finds the best substring
token_set_ratio; it ignores order and extra words, but any subset scores 100, so very short names can match too much
explain: token_set_ratio ignores word order and scores 100 when one word set contains the other, which absorbs added suffixes. The same property means a one-word name like `google` scores 100 against any longer name containing it, so pair it with a length check or a second score.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Geometric hashing: basis pairs, a hash table, and votes
question: You switch from similarity transforms to full 2D affine transforms (adding shear and non-uniform scale). What changes in the scheme?
options: The basis needs three non-collinear points, so preprocessing grows from O(Mn^3) to O(Mn^4)
Nothing; two points still define the frame
Hashing no longer works and you must compare all models directly
You need a 3D hash table
explain: Affine maps have 6 degrees of freedom, so 3 points are needed to fix a frame (the overview lists a three-point basis for 2D affine). With c = 3 the preprocessing cost O(Mn^(c+1)) becomes O(Mn^4), and recognition must try ordered triples of scene points.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: From an accepted match to a WCS header, and the triangle alternative
question: A solved WCS has CD matrix entries giving sqrt(|det CD|) = 0.000556 degrees per pixel. What is the pixel scale in arcseconds?
options: 0.556 arcsec/px
33.4 arcsec/px
0.0333 arcsec/px
2.0 arcsec/px
explain: One degree is 3600 arcsec, so 0.000556 x 3600 = 2.0 arcsec per pixel. The square root of the determinant removes the rotation and leaves the linear scale.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Better cells on the sphere: S2 cubes and H3 hexagons
question: You aggregate ride pickups into cells and smooth each cell's count with its immediate neighbors. Why might you pick H3 over geohash here?
options: Every H3 cell's neighbors are all the same distance from it, so equal smoothing weights make sense
H3 cells all have exactly the same area at every resolution
H3 IDs sort so that every pair of neighbors has consecutive IDs
H3 has no pentagons, so every cell has 6 neighbors
explain: Hexagon neighbors are equidistant, unlike square cells, whose diagonal neighbors are farther than edge neighbors. H3 cell areas vary (up to about 2 times within a resolution), no ordering makes all neighbors consecutive, and every resolution has exactly 12 pentagons with 5 neighbors each.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Warp and affine: an inverse map plus a border rule
question: Why do warp kernels evaluate the inverse transform rather than the forward one?
options: Because the inverse matrix has fewer coefficients, so it costs fewer FMAs
Because a forward scatter writes conflicting pixels and leaves destination holes, while an inverse gather writes each output exactly once
Because only the inverse map can be combined with interpolation
Because the forward map needs atomics for correctness, and atomics are unavailable in image kernels
explain: The gather form gives every destination pixel exactly one owning thread: no write conflicts, no holes, coalesced stores. Rounding the 16 pixels of a 30 degree rotated 4x4 forward fills only 12 of its 16 output cells. The inverse matrix is the same size as the forward one, and interpolation works in either direction, so neither of the other reasons holds.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
question: A script deletes its only large tensor and nvidia-smi still shows the same usage. What best explains this?
options: The tensor leaked because Python did not run its destructor
The caching allocator kept the freed block in its pool, so the memory is still reserved
cudaFree is asynchronous and will finish on the next kernel launch
nvidia-smi only refreshes once per training step
explain: With caching, a free returns the block to PyTorch's pool, not to the driver. memory_allocated() drops; memory_reserved() and nvidia-smi do not until empty_cache() or an OOM retry releases whole free segments.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Fixed-size suballocation for the KV cache, and diagnosing OOMs
question: Why does a pool of equal-size KV blocks have no external fragmentation?
options: Because blocks are always allocated at adjacent addresses
Because the GPU defragments memory in the background
Because any free block can satisfy any request for a block, so free memory is never too scattered to use
Because each request's maximum length is reserved up front
explain: External fragmentation means free memory exists but not in a usable shape. With one block size and a block table for indirection, any free block is usable by any request, so all free blocks count.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts
question: You pad a tile to `__shared__ float t[32][34];` and a warp reads `t[threadIdx.x][5]`. What happens?
options: No conflict, because the tile is padded
A 2-way bank conflict
A 32-way bank conflict
A broadcast, because every thread uses column 5
explain: Thread i reads word 34i + 5, bank (2i + 5) mod 32. Only 16 banks are used, each by two different words, so the greatest common divisor of 34 and 32, which is 2, gives 2 passes. Odd widths like 33 avoid it.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Occupancy: what it buys and what caps it
question: Theoretical occupancy is 75 percent but achieved occupancy is 31 percent. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The launch configuration is wrong and should use smaller blocks
The register allocation granularity was not accounted for
Shared memory is the real limiter rather than registers
The work is unbalanced: blocks differ a lot in cost, or most SMs are idle during a long tail
explain: Theoretical occupancy is what the launch configuration allows; achieved occupancy is the time average the hardware reached. Nsight Compute's own Occupancy section says large discrepancies between theoretical and achieved occupancy typically indicate highly imbalanced workloads. Check waves per SM and the per-SM active-cycle spread before touching registers or block size.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Computing a thread's global index: vector add end to end
question: In a 2D launch with blockDim = (16, 16), which pair of threads in the same block are neighbors in the linear thread order?
options: threadIdx (3, 5) and (3, 6)
threadIdx (3, 5) and (5, 3)
No pair: 2D blocks have no linear order
threadIdx (3, 5) and (4, 5)
explain: x moves fastest. (3, 5) has linear id 3 + 5 x 16 = 83 and (4, 5) has 84. Moving one step in y jumps by blockDim.x = 16.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
question: Which question is the best fit for GraphRAG's global search rather than plain vector RAG?
options: What year was Quillfern Labs founded?
Across all 2,000 support tickets, what recurring complaint themes appear?
Which supplier makes the Rover X2 drive motors?
What is Ben Ortiz's job title?
explain: The ticket-themes question needs a summary over the whole corpus, with no single chunk similar to the query. The other three are local fact lookups that top-k retrieval answers well and more cheaply.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured
question: A team reports "GraphRAG wins 80% of the time" using an LLM judge on comprehensiveness only. What is the best follow-up check, following the paper's design?
options: Nothing, 80% is decisive
Switch the judge to a smaller model
Remove the questions where GraphRAG lost
Also report a control criterion like directness, and validate with a judge-independent measure such as claim counts
explain: The paper adds directness as a control (vector RAG should win it, and does) and validates comprehensiveness and diversity with claim extraction. LLM judges have biases, so a sanity check matters.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Why PPO is costly for LLMs and what GRPO removes
question: Why is training a per-token critic especially awkward for LLM reasoning tasks?
options: Tokens are discrete, so value functions cannot be defined
Critics cannot be initialized from pretrained models
Value models require a larger vocabulary
The reward usually arrives only at the final token, so the critic must predict a distant outcome from every partial answer
explain: With an outcome reward at the end of a long chain of thought, the critic must predict from each prefix whether the final answer will be right, a hard regression problem. DeepSeekMath cites this as a motivation for GRPO.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Failure modes and fixes: dead groups, entropy collapse, length bias
question: Under the original GRPO normalization, two wrong answers have the same advantage -1, one with 100 tokens and one with 1,000. How does the per-token push-down compare?
options: Equal per token
The 1,000-token answer's tokens are pushed down 10 times more each
Wrong answers get no gradient in GRPO
The 1,000-token answer's tokens are pushed down 10 times less each
explain: Each output's token terms are divided by its length, so each token of the long answer gets one tenth of the weight. Long wrong answers are cheap, which can drive response length up. Token-level (DAPO) or constant (Dr. GRPO) normalization removes this.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Joining realtime to the schedule and propagating delay
question: A StopTimeUpdate has arrival.time = 1783343700 and arrival.delay = 0 (both present). The scheduled instant is 1783343580. Which prediction do you use?
options: 1783343700, because time takes precedence over delay
1783343580, because delay 0 means on time
The average of the two
Neither, the update is invalid and must be dropped
explain: The reference says that if both are given, time takes precedence, and normally time should equal scheduled time plus delay. Here they disagree (time implies +120 s), which is a data quality problem worth logging, but time wins.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf stat: counting, multiplexing and scaled estimates
question: A pinned event cannot get a counter. What does the perf_event_open man page say happens?
options: It goes into an error state and read returns end-of-file until it is re-enabled
It is multiplexed like any other event
The kernel evicts the NMI watchdog to make room
The count is silently reported as zero forever
explain: Pinned asks for the event to always be on the PMU. If that is impossible it does not fall back to multiplexing: it enters an error state where read(2) returns 0 bytes until it is disabled and enabled again.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Timing attacks on RSA: Kocher 1996 and remote timing in 2003
question: A team proposes adding a random 0 to 50 ms delay to every RSA operation instead of enabling blinding. What is the best response?
options: Accept: random delay makes timing attacks impossible
Accept, as long as the delay uses a cryptographic random generator
Reject, because delays are slower than blinding in every case
Reject: noise only multiplies the samples needed (roughly by the square of the noise), while blinding removes the attacker's knowledge of the input
explain: Kocher's analysis: samples needed grow with the square of the noise, so a patient attacker averages it away. Blinding breaks the link between the chosen input and what is exponentiated.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Spectre variant 1: speculating past a bounds check
question: In the Spectre v1 pattern, why is the secret byte multiplied by 4096 before indexing array2?
options: To encrypt it
Because pages must be accessed in order
To make the load slower and easier to time
So each possible value touches a different cache line and page, and the prefetcher does not pull in neighbours
explain: The covert channel needs one distinct, cleanly separated cache line per value. A 4096-byte stride puts each value on its own page, which also defeats prefetching across page boundaries.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Rowhammer: flipping bits in memory you never wrote
question: Why did the 2015 kernel exploit target page-table entries specifically?
options: One flipped bit in a PTE can redirect it to a page table the attacker controls, giving read-write access to all physical memory
Page tables are stored in the CPU cache, which is easier to hammer
PTEs are protected by ECC
The kernel rereads page tables every 64 ms
explain: A PTE holds a physical page number; flipping a low bit makes it point elsewhere. If it lands on one of the attacker's own page tables (memory was sprayed with them), the attacker can map any physical page.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Hardware supply chain, coordinated disclosure, and practice
question: Your company's code-signing tokens are found to contain an Infineon chip affected by ROCA. What is the necessary response?
options: Apply a firmware update; existing keys are then safe
Generate new keys on unaffected hardware and revoke the old public keys, because the existing keys can be factored from the public key alone
Nothing, because the tokens are FIPS 140-2 certified
Increase the RSA key length in the existing certificates
explain: ROCA's flaw is in how the primes were generated. Anyone with the public key can attempt the factorisation, so the keys themselves are weak: regenerate and revoke. Certification did not catch it.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Choosing, verifying and debugging huge pages in production
question: A JVM's 32 GiB heap shows AnonHugePages: 0 kB in smaps. THP enabled is set to madvise and defrag to madvise. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The heap is too large for THP
AnonHugePages only counts hugetlbfs pages
khugepaged has not had time to scan 32 GiB yet
The JVM did not mark the heap with madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE), so THP never applies to it
explain: In madvise mode only regions marked with MADV_HUGEPAGE are eligible, at fault time or for khugepaged. An unmarked heap gets zero THP no matter how long you wait. AnonHugePages counts PMD-mapped anonymous THP, not hugetlbfs, and there is no size limit.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: How Jamba, Nemotron-H and Qwen3-Next stack their layers
question: Why does Nemotron-H place a Mamba-2 layer first and use no RoPE in its attention layers?
options: RoPE is incompatible with grouped-query attention
The first Mamba-2 layer is recurrent and naturally encodes position, so explicit position embeddings are not needed
Attention layers at the start would make the KV cache grow quadratically
Mamba-2 layers require RoPE inputs and must come before attention
explain: Waleffe et al. put a Mamba layer at the start so the hybrid can work without position embeddings, since the recurrence itself depends on order. Their 840M ablation also found the hybrid without RoPE did better after long-context extension (continued training on longer sequences to raise the usable context).

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: A cross-encoder reranks the fused shortlist
question: Your hybrid pipeline reranks the top 20 fused results. Offline analysis shows many relevant documents sit at fused ranks 25 to 60. Which change addresses this most directly?
options: Increase rerank depth N (and possibly each retriever's window) if latency allows
Switch the cross-encoder to a larger model
Lower RRF's k to 1
Remove the BM25 retriever
explain: A better reranker cannot score documents it never sees. Raising N (and the per-retriever windows feeding fusion) brings them into reach; the cost is one more cross-encoder pass per added candidate.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Worked toy: how averaging fake answers changes the ranking
question: In the simple model with s = 1 and b = 0.3, going from N = 8 to N = 16 samples moves the cosine from about 0.91 to about 0.93. What does this suggest?
options: Always use N = 16
Shared bias is the main error, so prompt changes cannot help
Most of the remaining gap is the shared bias, so doubling generation cost buys little
Averaging hurts beyond N = 8
explain: The ceiling is 1 over the square root of 1.09, about 0.96. Past N = 8 the independent noise is already small, so extra samples cost tokens for a small gain. Reducing the shared bias (a clearer instruction, keeping the query in the average) is the better lever.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Inside a plant: sensors, PLCs, RTUs, HMIs, historians and SIS
question: Which machine would an attacker most want in order to change a PLC's program, and so which deserves the strongest protection?
options: The data historian
A sensor
The HMI's display monitor
The engineering workstation
explain: The engineering workstation holds the programming software and project files and can download logic to controllers. Stuxnet and Triton both worked through such machines.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: DNP3, S7comm and OPC UA: from no security to secure by design
question: A utility enables DNP3 Secure Authentication. An attacker can still sniff the link. What can they still do?
options: Read the measurements and commands in clear text, but not forge or replay critical commands without the key
Nothing: SAv5 encrypts all traffic
Forge operate commands because SAv5 only checks the master's IP
Change the MAC algorithm
explain: SAv5 authenticates critical messages with a challenge and MAC, defeating spoofing, modification and replay, but its spec says it addresses authentication only, not encryption. Confidentiality needs TLS or link encryptors.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Triton and the attack on a safety system
question: Mandiant notes the attacker already had a foothold on the DCS and could have shut the plant down from there. Why go after the SIS instead?
options: Compromising both control and safety could let them create a hazard while preventing the safety system from stopping it, causing physical damage
The SIS stores billing data
The SIS was easier to reach
To install ransomware
explain: Mandiant judged the long-term goal was a physical consequence. Shutting a plant down costs money; disabling the SIS while the DCS drives the process into an unsafe state could destroy equipment or harm people.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Incident response in OT: safety first, then manual
question: During an incident, the security lead wants to disconnect the control network immediately. What should happen first according to NIST's OT guidance?
options: A focused risk assessment with operations: confirm the process is safe and that operators can run it manually or without the network, then isolate
Disconnect immediately; safety is someone else's job
Wait until the next planned outage
Reboot every HMI to clear the infection
explain: NIST notes isolation may harm operational performance or safety and calls for a focused risk assessment to pick the response. Moving to manual operation first often makes isolation safe.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
question: Applying Otsu to the difference of two aligned photos where nothing changed (only sensor noise), what do you expect?
options: An empty mask, because Otsu detects that there is only one class
An error from OpenCV
A mask flagging a sizable fraction of noise pixels
A mask with exactly one pixel
explain: Otsu has no notion of 'one class'. It maximizes between-class variance over all splits, which always exists, so it will cut the noise distribution somewhere near its middle. Guard against this with a minimum threshold or a test on the gap between class means.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: The IR lifecycle: NIST 800-61r3, CSF 2.0 and SANS PICERL
question: In the SANS PICERL model, why does containment include a "system back-up" step before long-term containment?
options: To restore the user's files faster
To take a forensic image of affected systems before they are wiped or rebuilt, preserving evidence
Because backups are required before any patch
To test the backup software
explain: The handbook places a forensic image (it names commercial forensic imaging tools such as FTK (Forensic Toolkit) and EnCase) before wiping and reimaging, so the evidence survives for prosecution or for the lessons-learned analysis.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Evidence first: the order of volatility (RFC 3227)
question: RFC 3227 asks you to record the difference between the system clock and UTC. Why?
options: To meet a legal formatting rule
Because UTC is more secure
To detect whether the attacker changed the time zone
So that timestamps from this system can be aligned with other sources when building a timeline
explain: Timelines merge events from many machines. A server whose clock is 4 minutes fast puts its events in the wrong order relative to the firewall unless you record and correct the drift.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Linux artefacts: shell history, auth logs, cron, systemd, timestamps
question: A compromised server's /root/.bash_history has no commands from the intrusion window. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The attacker never used a root shell
Nothing: history is written at shell exit, can be disabled or redirected, and may never have been saved
The history file must have been edited
Root logins are not recorded by Linux
explain: Missing history is an absence of evidence, not evidence of absence. Look for other sources: auth logs, the journal, process accounting if enabled, file timestamps, and memory.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Ransomware response: pay or not, law enforcement and sanctions
question: During the 2017 NotPetya outbreak, a victim pays the ransom. What happens, according to Kaspersky's analysis?
options: They get a working key within hours
Nothing useful: the installation ID was random, so the attackers had no way to produce a key for that disk
Only the master boot record is restored
The payment is automatically refunded
explain: Kaspersky found the installation ID that a real ransomware operator needs for key recovery was generated from random data. NotPetya was a wiper presented as ransomware.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: When data becomes code: the one idea behind every injection
question: A program reads a city name and runs `eval("lookup('" + city + "')")`. A user types `Paris`. Another types `x') or delete_all('`. What does the second input do?
options: Nothing, because the city name is inside quotes
Python raises an error because quotes are not allowed in strings
It closes the quoted string early and adds a second function call to the expression
It only looks up a city literally named with those characters
explain: The built string becomes lookup('x') or delete_all(''). The first quote in the input closes the string literal the programmer opened, so the rest is parsed as code. Quotes only protect data if the data cannot contain the closing quote.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Heartland and TalkTalk: SQL injection as the way in
question: The ICO found that TalkTalk's vulnerable pages came from Tiscali, which it had acquired years earlier. Which control most directly addresses that root cause?
options: A longer password policy for staff
Encrypting backups
An inventory of every web application you expose, including acquired ones, with owners who patch and test them
Moving the database to a different vendor
explain: The pages were vulnerable, unpatched and apparently unknown to the people responsible. Knowing what you run, and giving each system an owner, is the precondition for fixing it.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: MOVEit 2023: one SQL injection, thousands of victims
question: You patched MOVEit on 3 June 2023. What should you do next?
options: Nothing: the patch removes the vulnerability and any damage
Rotate the TLS certificate
Hunt for signs of earlier compromise, such as human2.aspx files, "Health Check Service" accounts and unusual requests in web logs
Switch the database engine
explain: Exploitation began on 27 May, before any patch existed. A web shell installed before patching keeps working afterwards, so you must look for persistence and data theft, then remove and report them.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Server-side template injection
question:
Which change fixes `render_template_string("

" + request.args["title"] + "

")` in a Flask (Python web framework) app?
options: Turn on autoescape
Strip the characters { and } from title

Use a constant template and pass title as a variable: render_template_string("

{{ title }}

", title=request.args["title"])
Use HTTPS
explain: The fix moves the input from template source to template data. Autoescape only affects output encoding, and stripping braces is a denylist that may miss other syntax such as {% %} or engine-specific forms.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Two shared rings: SQEs, CQEs, head and tail
question: A 4-entry SQ has tail counter 9. Which slot does the next SQE go into?
options: Slot 1, because 9 & 3 = 1
Slot 9, the tail value
Slot 0, because the ring is full after 4
Slot 2, because the next SQE goes one past the tail: 10 & 3 = 2
explain: The slot is `tail & (entries - 1)` = 9 & 3 = 1. The tail counter itself is never reset; it just keeps counting and the mask wraps it onto the 4 slots.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: jemalloc: arenas, tcache, bitmap slabs and decay purging
question: Using jemalloc's rule, how big is the slab for the 96-byte class with 4 KiB pages?
options: 3 pages, 128 regions, no waste
1 page, 42 regions, 64 bytes wasted
2 pages, 85 regions
96 pages, 4,096 regions
explain: lcm(4096, 96) = 12,288 bytes = 3 pages, and 12,288 / 96 = 128 regions exactly. A 1-page slab would leave 4096 - 42 x 96 = 64 bytes unusable; jemalloc avoids that by growing the slab until the region size divides it.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Why a healthy cluster hides consistency bugs
question: A team runs its integration tests 10,000 times on a five-node cluster with no faults and never sees a lost write. What does that tell you about lost writes during a leader change?
options: They cannot happen, because 10,000 runs is statistically enough
They are impossible because Raft guarantees committed entries survive
Very little: leader changes never happened in those runs, so the code that handles them was barely exercised
They can only happen if the disk is corrupted
explain: Without injected faults the failure-handling paths rarely run at all. Raft's guarantee covers committed log entries; bugs often live around it, in reads served outside the log, client retries, or leases (time-limited grants that expire unless renewed). Repetition of a run that never triggers the path proves nothing about it.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions
question: Elle reports a cycle T1 wr T2, T2 rw T3, T3 rw T1. How is it classified?
options: G0, because it is a cycle
G1c, because it contains a wr edge
G2, because it has two rw edges
G-single, because it has exactly one rw edge
explain: The cycle has two anti-dependency (rw) edges, so it is G2 but not G-single. G1c cycles contain only ww and wr edges; G0 only ww. Two rw edges is the shape of write skew, which snapshot isolation allows but serializability forbids.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Measuring, caching and promoting without regressions
question: Your autotuning cache is keyed on (M, N, K, dtype). The team upgrades the GPU driver and compiler, and performance drops on some shapes. What is the most likely cause?
options: The cached winners were chosen under the old codegen and no key component changed, so nothing re-tuned
The new compiler produces slower code for every configuration equally
The cache capacity was exceeded and entries were evicted
The dtype hash changed, forcing a re-tune that picked worse configs
explain: Nothing in (M, N, K, dtype) reflects the toolchain, so every lookup still hits and serves a configuration that was optimal for the old compiler. This is why Triton's on-disk autotune cache hashes the Triton version, the backend hash and the relevant environment variables along with the tuning key and the config list.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Scaling across cores: one queue per core, rings and mempools
question: An rte_ring of size 16 has prod_tail = 3 and cons_head = 4294967295. How many entries does it hold?
options: It is corrupted: prod is behind cons
explain: (3 - 4294967295) mod 2^32 = 4. The producer counter simply wrapped past 2^32 - 1; unsigned 32-bit subtraction gives the right distance without any special case.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Vertical and horizontal fusion
question: Two sibling kernels each read a different 1 KB tensor. What does horizontal fusion mainly save?
options: Half of the HBM traffic
Nothing; fusion only helps when inputs are shared
One kernel launch's fixed overhead
Register pressure
explain: No bytes are shared, so traffic is unchanged. With tiny tensors the runtime is dominated by fixed launch cost, and merging two launches into one removes one of those costs.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Temperature: amplifying the small probabilities
question: At T = 1 the teacher thinks dog is 90 times more likely than car (logit gap 4.5). What is that ratio at T = 4?
options: 90, temperature preserves ratios
About 3.08, because the ratio is exp(4.5 / 4)
22.5, the ratio divides by T
1, every class becomes equally likely
explain: The probability ratio is exp of the logit gap divided by T: exp(4.5 / 4) = exp(1.125), about 3.08. Temperature divides the logit gap, so the probability ratio shrinks exponentially, not linearly. The ordering is preserved; the ratio is not.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
question: You want to distill a model whose tokenizer differs from your student's. Which approach works without extra machinery?
options: Word-level KD, matching probabilities token by token
Sequence-level KD on the teacher's generated text, re-tokenized by the student
Logit matching with squared error
Reverse-KL on-policy distillation
explain: Token-level losses compare distributions over the same vocabulary at the same positions, which a different tokenizer breaks. Generated text is tokenizer-neutral: the student can tokenize it its own way and train with ordinary cross-entropy.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production
question: Your FP8 KV cache (no calibration) is accurate on most layers but one sliding-window layer degrades. Which change targets that directly?
options: Switch every layer to 2-bit KIVI
Increase the batch size
Use FP8 e5m2 for weights
Keep that layer's cache in the native dtype and the rest in FP8
explain: vLLM documents a skip-layers option for exactly this: sensitive layers stay in the model's dtype while the rest use the quantized cache.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Reload or recompute: bytes versus prefill FLOPs
question: A colleague says: 'Prefill cost grows faster than load cost as prompts get longer, so offloading pays off more for long prompts.' Which part of the cost model makes this true?
options: KV bytes per token grow with prompt length
The attention term in prefill grows with $n^2$ while bytes grow with $n$
Longer prompts compress better on disk
PCIe bandwidth increases for larger transfers
explain: Every token stores the same 131,072 bytes, so load time is linear in $n$. Prefill has the linear-layer term $2Pn$ plus causal attention $2Ldn^2$, which dominates at long lengths. That is why even a 1 GB/s object store beats prefill beyond about 147K tokens in this model.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Why wall clocks cannot order events across machines
question: A team proposes fixing the lost write by running NTP more often so clocks stay within 1 ms. What is the remaining problem?
options: None: with 1 ms skew last write wins is always correct
NTP cannot run more often than once per hour
Two causally ordered writes less than the skew apart can still get reversed timestamps, and NTP can still step a clock
Last write wins only fails when clocks run slow, never fast
explain: Tighter sync shrinks the window but does not close it. Any two causally related writes closer together than the current skew can be misordered, and NTP gives no hard guarantee: the paper cites occasional errors of 100 ms or more, and stepping can move a clock backwards.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: HLC in production: 64 bits, bounded c, and uncertainty
question: Why does the paper keep l and c in separate fields instead of using the naive single counter max(l+1, l.m+1, pt)?
options: To save space: two fields are smaller than one
So l can always be reset back to pt when the physical clock catches up, keeping l minus pt bounded, while c carries the tie-breaking
Because vector clocks require two fields
So c can track the number of nodes in the cluster
explain: In the naive version the +1s are mixed into the same number as physical time, so l can drift arbitrarily far ahead. Separating them lets HLC throw away the counter (c = 0) whenever pt or a message brings a new, larger l, which is what bounds both l minus pt and c.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Storage: why token vectors are heavy and how ColBERTv2 shrinks them
question: Why does residual compression work so well on ColBERT vectors specifically?
options: ColBERT vectors are binary to begin with
MaxSim ignores all but the first few dimensions
Token vectors cluster tightly by word sense, so the residual from the nearest centroid is small and survives coarse quantization
The centroids are stored at 1 bit per dimension
explain: The paper's cluster analysis shows contextual token vectors concentrate near centroids that each hold a few related tokens. Small residuals lose little when cut to 2 or 1 bits per dimension. Random vectors do not cluster like this, so they would compress worse.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: The continuous thought: hidden state in, hidden state out
question: The GSM8k Coconut model uses c = 2 thoughts per reasoning step and 3 latent stages, so its final stage has 6 thoughts. How many sequential forward passes does one training example in that stage need?
options: 1, because training uses teacher forcing
explain: n latent thoughts need n passes to create them plus one more pass to score the remaining tokens: 6 + 1 = 7. Teacher forcing cannot help, because the inputs at the latent slots do not exist until the previous pass has run.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: The last mile and the Recursive Model Index
question: You double the number of leaf models in a 2-stage RMI from 10,000 to 20,000. What happens to the per-lookup work of evaluating models?
options: It stays the same: one stage-0 model and one leaf model per lookup
It roughly doubles, because the top model must compare against twice as many leaves
It grows by one level, like adding a level to a B-tree
It halves, because each leaf covers half as many keys
explain: Routing is arithmetic: floor(M x f0(x) / N) jumps straight to a leaf, whatever M is. More leaves cost memory and can tighten error windows, which can shorten the final search, but model evaluation stays one model per stage.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Inserts, disks and when a learned index pays off
question: A table's keys are inserted in an order whose distribution differs sharply from the keys already loaded. In ALEX, what is the main risk and the built-in response?
options: The model becomes inaccurate, leaving long runs with no gaps; ALEX detects the cost drift and splits or retrains nodes
Keys are lost because model-based insertion overwrites slots
Deletes slow down because they must shift keys
Nothing, because exponential search makes model accuracy irrelevant
explain: Model-based insertion depends on the model; if new keys do not follow it, they pile up and create long contiguous runs where every insert shifts many keys and searches go further. ALEX compares observed cost with the expected cost from its cost models and then expands with retraining or splits the node.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: SPLADE v2, SPLADE++ and running it in production
question: You need the lowest query latency on CPU-only search nodes but still want expansion. Which setup fits best?
options: Bi-encoder SPLADE with lambda_q = 0
Dense retrieval with HNSW
Doc-only sparse mode: expand documents at index time, tokenize queries with fixed weights
BM25 with doc length normalization disabled
explain: Doc-only mode keeps expansion on the document side, computed offline, and runs no transformer at query time. lambda_q = 0 would make queries denser and slower.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaMART: boosted trees that fit the lambdas
question: Which statement about what one LambdaMART tree learns is correct?
options: It predicts each document's relevance label
It predicts NDCG for each query
It predicts the per-document lambdas from the features, pooled over all queries
It learns a separate tree for each query
explain: The regression targets are the lambdas, and Burges stresses that each tree models the lambdas for the entire dataset, not a single query. Labels enter only through |delta NDCG|.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The delta rule: overwrite instead of add
question: Memory holds $k_A\to4$ and $k_B\to2$ with orthogonal unit keys. A token writes $k_A\to1$ with $\beta=1$ using the delta rule. What does $k_B$ read afterwards?
explain: The update only changes $S$ along $k_A$: $S(I-k_Ak_A^\top)$ leaves the $k_B$ direction untouched because $k_A^\top k_B=0$. So $k_B$ still reads 2, while $k_A$ now reads exactly 1.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Users, groups and root: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
question: Why is /etc/passwd readable by every user while /etc/shadow is readable only by root?
options: Programs everywhere need to map UIDs to names, but password hashes can be guessed offline if copied
Because /etc/passwd is encrypted and /etc/shadow is not
It is a historical accident with no security effect
So that users can change other users' passwords
explain: Name and UID lookups happen constantly, so passwd must be public. A copied hash can be attacked with unlimited offline guesses, so hashes were moved to shadow, which is unreadable to ordinary users.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Processes, PIDs, process trees and signals
question: Which observation is the strongest sign of compromise on a web server?
options: sshd running as root with PPID 1
bash running as www-data whose parent is an apache2 worker
A process named kworker
cron running as root
explain: sshd under PID 1 and cron as root are normal. Kernel threads are named kworker but have no executable. A shell spawned by a web server worker is the classic sign of command injection or a Shellshock-style bug.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: regreSSHion: a signal handler race in the SSH server
question: Why was LoginGraceTime 0 an effective emergency mitigation for regreSSHion?
options: With no login time limit, the SIGALRM handler never fires, so there is no race to win
It disables password login
It makes sshd use syslog_r()
It blocks all unauthenticated connections
explain: The vulnerable code only runs when the grace-time alarm goes off. A value of 0 means no limit, so no alarm. The cost is that idle unauthenticated connections can exhaust MaxStartups (sshd's limit on connections still waiting to log in) and deny service.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Why relevance labels are the bottleneck of search evaluation
question: A team has 2,000 queries and 40 ranker variants per week, and wants NDCG@10 for all of them. What is the main reason they consider an LLM judge?
options: NDCG cannot be computed from human labels
Each new variant surfaces unjudged documents, and human labels for all of them are too slow and costly
LLM labels are always more accurate than human labels
LLMs can compute NDCG directly without labels
explain: NDCG needs a grade for every returned document. New rankers keep surfacing unjudged documents, so the labelling bill grows with every experiment. The LLM judge makes that bill small. Accuracy is not automatic: it has to be checked against gold labels.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Judge biases: position, verbosity and self-preference
question: A colleague adds an "include more detail" step to the generator in a RAG system, and the LLM judge's preference for its answers rises from 50% to 70%. Which explanation should you rule out before celebrating?
options: Verbosity bias: the judge may be rewarding length rather than better content
Position bias in the generator
Kendall's tau is too low
The gold set is too large
explain: Zheng et al.'s repetitive list attack shows weaker judges preferring padded answers over 90% of the time. Check with length-controlled comparisons or human spot checks before attributing the gain to quality.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: LLM judges for generation: modes, biases and fixes
question: Which mitigation targets position bias specifically?
options: Using a judge from a different model family
Fitting a tanh length term
Evaluating both orders and combining the results
Adding a reference answer to the prompt
explain: Balanced Position Calibration (Wang et al.) and swap-and-tie (Zheng et al.) run both orders so that position effects cancel or show up as ties. A different-family judge targets self-preference; the length term targets verbosity.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Threat model: how an LLM app gets attacked or goes wrong
question: An email assistant reads the user's inbox and can send emails. Which threat is the most direct route to it sending data to an attacker?
options: A jailbreak typed by the user
Hallucinated claims in a summary
Indirect prompt injection in an incoming email
A slow model response
explain: The attacker only needs to send an email: the assistant reads it as context, and injected instructions plus a send-email tool give a path to exfiltration. A user jailbreak needs the user to be the attacker; hallucination does not move data out.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Measuring a guard, and why no guard is complete
question: A vendor reports their jailbreak detector blocks 99% of attacks in a public benchmark. What is the most important question before relying on it?
options: Which GPU it runs on
Whether it uses a transformer
How it performs against adaptive attacks crafted against it, and what its false positive rate is on your traffic
Whether the benchmark is in English
explain: Static benchmarks measure known attacks. Studies such as Zou et al. and Hackett et al. show optimized or obfuscated inputs evade guards, and the FPR on your own base rate decides how many real users get blocked.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables
question: Paging lets a server admit a request after allocating only its prompt's blocks. What new problem does this create that max-length reservation did not have?
options: Requests can no longer share a batch
The pool can run out in the middle of generation, when running requests need new blocks that are not there
Prompts longer than one block cannot be stored
Block tables use more memory than the KV cache itself
explain: Reservation guaranteed every admitted request could finish. Allocating on demand bets that not everyone will grow at once; when the bet loses, some running request has nowhere to put its next token. Handling that is the job of preemption, the next lesson.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Few-shot examples and asking the model to reason first
question: With manual chain-of-thought, your code needs only the final number. What does Anthropic suggest?
options: Ask for the answer first, then the reasoning
Forbid reasoning so the output is just the number
Ask for reasoning first and the final answer inside <answer> tags, then extract the tags
Parse the last number that appears anywhere in the response
explain: Reasoning first keeps the benefit; a fixed delimiter makes extraction reliable. Answer-first loses the benefit, and grabbing the last number breaks as soon as the model mentions a number after its answer.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Why hard constraints need filters, not similarity
question: LangChain's default few-shot prompt includes the question *What are songs that were not published on Spotify* for a data source whose only fields are artist, length and genre. What filter does the example answer give?
options: and(ne("platform", "Spotify"))
NO_FILTER, because no field records the platform
not(contain("artist", "Spotify"))
It refuses to answer the query
explain: The example answer is query "" with filter NO_FILTER. The prompt also instructs the model that filters may only refer to attributes that exist. Inventing a platform field would produce a query the store cannot run, or one that silently matches nothing.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Latency budgets, caching and parallel fallback
question: To benefit from prompt prefix caching, where should the user's query go in the parser prompt?
options: At the end, after the instructions, field descriptions and examples
At the start, so the model reads it first
In the middle, between instructions and examples
It does not matter, caching hashes the whole prompt
explain: Caching reuses a matching prefix, so everything identical across requests should come first and the part that changes every time should come last. A query at the start changes the prefix on every request and nothing is reused.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Cutting decode: FIRST and single-token listwise ranking
question: Why does the relative saving of FIRST shrink when passages get longer?
options: Longer passages make the first-token logits less accurate
FIRST must generate more tokens for long passages
Prefill grows with L while the decode time saved stays the same, so the saved share falls
Long passages force smaller windows
explain: The saved part is (t_id m - 1) x TPOT, which does not depend on L. Prefill, which both methods pay, grows with mL.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pointwise: yes/no relevance and query likelihood
question: Two passages get p(Yes) = 0.83 and 0.79 from separate calls. Why might the lower one still be the better passage?
options: Each score is produced in isolation, so small differences reflect calibration noise rather than a real comparison
p(Yes) is always inversely related to relevance
Sorting requires scores to sum to 1
The second call used fewer tokens
explain: The model never saw the two passages side by side. Its probability depends on passage length, wording and prompt quirks, so a 0.04 gap is not a reliable comparison. Pairwise and listwise prompts address exactly this.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Position bias, robustness and distilled rerankers
question: Why did RankGPT's distilled 440M DeBERTa reranker beat its ChatGPT teacher on BEIR?
options: It was trained on human relevance labels as well
It ranks each passage with a stable deterministic score instead of an occasionally malformed or inconsistent permutation
It used a longer context window than ChatGPT
It reranked 1000 passages instead of 100
explain: The student learns the teacher's preferences through a pairwise RankNet loss but scores each passage with a deterministic forward pass, so it avoids the teacher's missing ids, repetitions and window-to-window inconsistency. The authors attribute the gap to this stability.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Managed routing in Amazon Bedrock, and how routers fail
question: After launching in Japan, your router's share of strong-model calls drops from 35% to 12% and complaints about answer quality rise. What is the most likely cause?
options: The strong model became cheaper
Input distribution shift: the router misjudges the difficulty of prompts unlike its training data and sends hard ones to the weak model
Judge bias toward longer answers
The router's GPU is overloaded
explain: A sudden change in routing mix plus worse quality right after new traffic arrives points to drift. Bedrock's docs say its routing is optimized only for English prompts, and RouteLLM's routers fell to near random on out-of-distribution benchmarks.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: RANSAC: keeping only matches that agree on one homography
question: Inlier ratio is 0.5 and you need 99% confidence. How many RANSAC iterations does a homography (s = 4) need?
explain: N = log(0.01)/log(1 - 0.5^4) = log(0.01)/log(0.9375) = 71.36, rounded up to 72. 16 is 1/w^4, the expected number of draws to see the first clean sample, which is not enough for 99% confidence. 567 is the answer for w = 0.3.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Michael-Scott queue: a dummy node and helping
question: A thread in enqueue reads Tail = X and finds X.next is not NULL. What does the algorithm do?
options: Wait until the thread that linked X.next swings Tail
Try to CAS Tail forward to X.next, then retry its own enqueue
Link its node after X anyway
Return failure because the queue is full
explain: That is E13: Tail is lagging, so the thread helps advance it and loops. Waiting would make the algorithm blocking, and linking after X would break the list because X is not the last node.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Why one regular expression per format does not scale
question: Why is "88 percent of Thunderbird's templates are missing from a 2,000-line sample" a problem for a hand-written regex set, but not fatal for a template miner?
options: The miner has already seen all 1,241 templates during training
The miner stores raw lines, so it can re-derive templates on demand
The miner creates a new template group the first time it sees an unmatched line, so unseen formats cost nothing extra
Rare templates are noise and a miner correctly discards them
explain: An online miner's whole job is to open a new group for a line that matches nothing. A regex set has to be edited by a person before the new format parses at all, and until then those lines fall into an unparsed bucket. Rare templates are usually the valuable ones: error-level messages are rare by construction.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drift when a release changes the format, and a pipeline that holds
question: Your log volume quadruples and the parser falls behind. Which of the Huawei deployment's four measures gives both a throughput win and an accuracy win?
options: Partitioning by verbosity level and component, since different levels and components come from different logging statements: fewer candidates per partition, and the partitions parse in parallel
Raising the similarity threshold so fewer comparisons are needed
Reducing the tree depth to shorten every walk
Sampling one line in four and extrapolating the counts
explain: Partitioning narrows the search space, which speeds parsing, and it also removes the chance of merging templates across components, which helps accuracy. It is also the parallelization key they used with Spark. Threshold and depth are accuracy trade-offs, not free wins, and sampling destroys exactly the rare error templates you most want to count.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: The pipeline: collect, ship, parse, enrich, store
question: At Equifax, what would most directly have shortened the 76 days?
options: A new Sigma rule for Struts exploits
An alert when an inspection device stops decrypting (expired certificate) or its sensors stop producing alerts
Longer log retention
Moving the IDS in front of the SSLV device
explain: The detection layer was fine once it could see. What failed was visibility, and nothing alerted on its loss. Monitoring sensor health (and owning certificate renewal) attacks the actual cause. An IDS in front of the decryptor would see only ciphertext.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: MITRE ATT&CK as a coverage map
question: A rule's tag is attack.t1059.001. What does it tell another engineer?
options: The rule's severity
Which ATT&CK sub-technique (PowerShell, under Command and Scripting Interpreter) the rule is meant to detect
The rule's Sigma version
The Windows event ID it reads
explain: Sigma tags use the attack namespace for ATT&CK. T1059.001 is the PowerShell sub-technique; tags let tools build coverage maps automatically.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Tuning and allowlisting without blinding yourself
question: A rule's alert count drops from 40 a day to 0 after a tuning change. What should you check first?
options: That the rule's must-match test cases still pass, and that the data source is still arriving
Nothing, the tuning worked perfectly
The SIEM licence
Whether analysts are happy
explain: Zero is suspicious. Either the filter is too broad (tests catch that), or the source went silent (pipeline health catches that). Both look like success.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Why models break past their trained length
question: In the toy head (wavelengths 6.3, 62.8, 628.3, 6,283 tokens; trained on 2,048), which pair sees an out-of-distribution angle first as the prompt grows past 2,048 tokens?
options: Pair 0, because it rotates fastest and accumulates the largest angle
Pair 3, because it never completed a full turn during training
All pairs equally, because every position past 2,048 is new
None, because RoPE only depends on relative distance
explain: Pair 0 reaches huge raw angles but wraps every 6.3 tokens, so every angle on its circle was seen thousands of times. Pair 3 only ever covered 0 to 2.047 rad, so at position 2,100 it is already at 2.1 rad, outside its training range.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Hiding communication, causal balance and Ulysses
question: Why does DeepSpeed Ulysses' per-link communication stay constant as you scale sequence length and GPU count together?
options: It compresses activations to 1 bit
It only communicates the KV cache once per training run
It never communicates; each GPU attends locally
An all-to-all over P GPUs moves M/P per link, and the message M = 4Nh grows with N at the same rate as P
explain: Per-link volume is 4Nh/P. Doubling both N and P leaves it unchanged. With h = 4096 and N = 32K tokens per GPU, that is about 1.07 GB per layer in bf16 at P = 2, 4, 8 or 16.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Training for any loop count: random depth and truncated backprop
question: Gradients flow only through the last 8 core iterations. Why does the prelude still get trained on every step?
options: It does not; the prelude is frozen after warm-up
Because the coda shares weights with the prelude
Because the no-grad iterations are re-run with gradients at the end of the step
